[eval r01] Reference note for this evaluation pass: prefix caches key on the exact token prefix, so this header exists to force a cold prefill on every rep.

The key-value cache is the quiet protagonist of every long-context inference stack. When a request arrives, the server tokenizes the prompt and, unless the prefix already lives in the cache, runs a full prefill pass over every input token before a single output token appears. That prefill phase is compute-bound: the arithmetic intensity is high, the matrix multiplications are wide, and the wall-clock cost scales roughly linearly with prompt length once attention overhead is amortized. The decode phase that follows is the opposite animal: memory-bandwidth-bound, one token at a time, each step rereading the entire weight set and the growing attention cache. A harness that measures the two phases together will report a number that means very little, which is why time-to-first-token and decode throughput are tracked as separate, independently gated metrics.

Prefix caching changes the economics of repeated prompts. If two requests share an identical token prefix, the server can reuse the cached key-value blocks for the shared region and skip recomputation entirely. This is a legitimate optimization in production, but it is a measurement hazard in a benchmark: a warm cache makes a prefill look artificially fast, and the speedup depends on traffic history rather than on the build under test. The mitigation is deliberate cache busting. Every prompt that is meant to exercise the prefill path must be unique enough, and different enough between repetitions, that no prior request in the process lifetime shares its leading blocks. A short, distinctive marker line at the very top of the prompt is the cheapest reliable way to guarantee this, because the cache matches from the first token onward; a single differing token at position zero poisons the entire shared prefix.

Quantization interacts with both phases in ways that a naive mental model gets wrong. Weight-only quantization such as Q4_0 shrinks the bytes that must stream from memory during decode, so decode throughput typically improves close to the compression ratio, modulo dequantization overhead in the kernel. Prefill, being compute-bound, benefits less and can even regress if the dequantization path is not fused well with the matmul. Numerical drift of this kind is exactly what a greedy seal catches: two builds that agree on the first dozen tokens can diverge catastrophically later, because a single flipped argmax at a near-tie changes every subsequent position. This is why the seal is a hash over the full normalized completion, not a fuzzy similarity score.

Batching and scheduling add another layer of measurement noise. A continuous-batching scheduler interleaves new requests with in-flight decodes, so the decode tokens-per-second observed by one request depends on who else was in the server at the time. Contamination from a neighbor job inflates variance, and the honest response to a high coefficient of variation is to quiesce the machine and rerun, never to widen the tolerance until the number fits.

Topology deserves its own paragraph because it is the fingerprint that changes most often between runs of the same nominal build. A two-GPU tensor-parallel pair behaves differently from a single device even when the model fits on one card: every layer boundary pays a reduction tax, the split of vocabulary-parallel work at the final projection is lopsided, and the interconnect path, whether PCIe with peer-to-peer enabled or routed through the root complex, sets the floor on per-token synchronization cost. NUMA placement of the host process, whether the weights are memory-locked against eviction, and whether flash attention is compiled in for the target architecture all belong in the same provenance record. When a seal is promoted, the record of what the machine looked like at promotion time is as important as the hash itself, because a later mismatch is only actionable if you can tell a configuration change apart from a code regression.

Finally, a note on why these long prompts are written as ordinary prose rather than synthetic filler. Tokenizers are strange compressors: repeated word-salad compresses into surprising token sequences, and a prompt assembled from shuffled vocabulary can tokenize in ways that no realistic workload ever would, quietly steering the measurement onto a degenerate path. Real technical prose, varied in sentence length and vocabulary, exercises the prefill path the way production traffic does. The three long prompts in this suite therefore carry distinct bodies and distinct marker lines, so a comparison between them measures the cache policy and the build, not the shape of the filler.
